reasoning: Extensive scientific research and double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have repeatedly failed to demonstrate a causal link between monosodium glutamate (MSG) consumed in normal dietary amounts and symptoms like headaches, numbness, or chest tightness. The concept of "Chinese restaurant syndrome" originated largely from an anecdotal 1968 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine, followed by flawed initial studies and anti-Asian xenophobia. Major regulatory and health organizations, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the World Health Organization (WHO), classify MSG as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS), confirming that the body metabolizes glutamate added as MSG in the exact same manner as glutamate naturally found in foods like tomatoes and parmesan cheese.
